questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: What trust is and how to decide who deserves it
How fake news is made and shared online
The life of a famous American financier
Why presidents often tell lies
questions.why: Rob says they'll discuss what trust is and who we should place our trust in.

questions.q: What has the coronavirus epidemic led to, according to Neil?
options: Much more trust in governments and scientists
People spending less time online than before
More misinformation and conspiracy theories online
Fewer news programmes on TV and the radio
questions.why: Neil says it has led to an increase in misinformation, lies and conspiracy theories on the internet.

questions.q: According to philosopher Onora O'Neill, what is the real problem?
options: People no longer trust anyone, even their families
There is far too little reliable information available
Trusting others makes life slower and more difficult
Not trust itself, but whether people are trustworthy
questions.why: Neil says she believes the problem is not about trust itself but about trustworthiness.

questions.q: What does Onora O'Neill say about trusting people without judging them first?
options: It is the best way to make friends
It is gullible and probably not a virtue
It makes society work better
It is only a problem in business
questions.why: She says placing trust indiscriminately is 'gullible' and 'probably not a virtue'.

questions.q: Why do the presenters mention Bernie Madoff?
options: As an example of people trusting without judgement
As an example of an honest, trustworthy businessman
To explain how the Trojan Horse trick really worked
To show that prison sentences for fraud are too long
questions.why: Rob says Madoff tricked people because they were gullible and trusted him indiscriminately.

questions.q: What three ingredients of trustworthiness does O'Neill identify?
options: Kindness, honesty and patience
Wealth, power and competence
Luck, honesty and friendship
Honesty, competence and reliability
questions.why: Rob says she identifies honesty, competence and reliability.

questions.q: Why does Neil talk about a car mechanic and a dentist?
options: To show that some jobs are more honest than others
To show that dentists earn much more than mechanics
To say we trust people only for what they're good at
To show that mechanics are more reliable than dentists
questions.why: He says you'd trust a mechanic to fix your car but not to remove a tooth, as they're not competent.

Something only large companies really need to worry about
Less important than honesty in most situations
The boring one: being honest and competent every time
questions.why: She calls it 'the boring one', meaning being honest and competent each time.
